power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p>0.001", Sentence = "Those who received integrated services were around 2.6 years younger, had on average around one child more, and were significantly less likely to report having HIV than those who did not receive integrated vFP and CCS (p>0.001) (Table 1)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. text.text: Introduction: Mozambique faces a significant burden of cervical cancer, but screening rates are currently low.
While voluntary family planning (vFP) services are more widely accessible, unmet need for contraception remains at 22%.
Integrating vFP and cervical cancer screening and preventive therapy (CCS&PT) services presents an opportunity to address these issues by improving service efficiency and reaching more women.
text.formatted: Integrating vFP and cervical cancer screening and preventive therapy (CCS&PT) services presents an opportunity to address these issues by improving service efficiency and reaching more women.

text.text: This paper examines the uptake, feasibility, and experiences of integrating vFP services into CCS&PT services in Mozambique.
text.formatted: This paper examines the uptake, feasibility, and experiences of integrating vFP services into CCS&PT services in Mozambique.

text.text: Methods: This mixed-methods operational research study was conducted in four public health facilities in Mozambique.

Quantitative data were collected from January 2020 to October 2022 as part of the MULHER study and included program monitoring data from clinical encounters (N=9,014) and client exit interviews (N=504).
Qualitative data was gathered through in-depth interviews (IDIs) with 60 clients and 15 providers in two phases, in October 2021 and November 2022.
Results: Out of 9,014 women eligible for HPV screening, 88% received both HPV screening and vFP counselling. 21% of these women took up a modern method of FP, 20% of whom were new users.
Multivariable analysis showed that the likelihood of receiving integrated services was significantly associated with a range of factors including parity, age and HIV status.
Qualitative data revealed that both clients and providers generally perceived the integrated model as beneficial.
Clients highlighted the convenience, enhanced privacy, reduced travel costs, and opportunity to learn about new services.
Providers emphasized similar benefits alongside the potential for increased demand through peer referrals.
Integrating voluntary family planning and cervical cancer screening and preventative treatment: lessons from the PEER project in Mozambique

Integrating voluntary family planning into cervical cancer screening service provision in Mozambique results in high levels of satisfaction among patients and providers and appears to make FP methods available to new users.

1) The study shows high levels of uptake of integrated vFP services among women enrolled in cervical screening and preventive therapy (CCS&PT) in the four public health facilities in Maputo and Gaza provinces, with almost 9 in 10 women who were enrolled for HPV screening also receiving vFP counselling on the day of their visit.

text.text: The components of the present study were designed to allow for triangulation of findings, with the objective of gaining a comprehensive view of the facilitators of and barriers to integration, and experiences of those who engaged with the project offering integrated cervical cancer screening and family planning provision.
The quantitative dataset presented here comprises program monitoring data from clinical encounters (N=9,014) and client exit interview data (N=504).
The program monitoring data were collected routinely during the implementation of the MULHER study (January 2020 to January 2023).
Women aged 30-49 were prospectively enrolled from January 2020 to October 2022 in Maputo City and Gaza province, Mozambique.
These client-level data were recorded in pen and paper client records by trained providers working in the PEER project.

They contained variables describing client characteristics, HPV sample type (self-sampling or provider collected sample), vFP counselling and FP product use, alongside information on hrHPV test results and subsequent follow-up.
All data was entered in REDCap (Harris et al., 2009), a web application for building and managing online surveys and databases.

Data collection occurred in two phases: the first wave (N clients=20) took place in October 2021, followed by second wave (N clients =40; N providers = 15) in November 2022.
Clients were recruited from waiting rooms, provided with a study overview, and enrolled upon giving written consent.

Among all HPV-screened women, mean age was 37.7 years (sd =5.5).
HIV positivity was 45.7%.
Among the 60% who reported education level, 43% had primary and 29% had secondary schooling.

text.text: Uptake of integrated vFP services among those eligible for cervical cancer screening (or hrHPV test) was high.
In total, 7,924 (88%) received both cervical cancer screening test and family planning counseling.
Among those who received cervical cancer screening and vFP counseling, 1,694 (21%) took up modern method of vFP (initiated, switched, continued) on the day of counseling.

text.text: Among FP method users, the FP method mix was dominated by injectables and oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) (63.7% and 25.8%, respectively), with long-acting reversible contraceptives (LARCs) reported by around 1 in 20 women (3.6% and 1.0% for implants and IUDs, respectively), and condoms accounting for the remainder (5.8%).

In-depth interviews with clients and providers aimed to establish the degree to which they considered the integrated CCS&PT and vFP services to be acceptable and feasible, and to explore any barriers or enablers in their access to the program.

text.text: In general, clients expressed positive opinions of the integration: "I am very happy with the way the services are going, on the same day at the same place and with the same nurse, I save a lot of things at the same time, I save time because I only have one trip to the hospital, I save money on transport, before I used to get twice and now I get once and come here and thirdly I feel comfortable because I only talk to one nurse about my issues" (Client, Jose Macamo health facility, Maputo province) Another said: "For me it [integration] is good the way it is because the users only have to expose their health problems to one health professional, they don't have to join queues to receive two services, unlike what happened a few years ago" (Client, Chibuto health facility, Gaza province) Integrated care is highlighted as having multiple cost and time benefits for clients, as well as the implied benefit of additional privacy brought by only having to discuss health issues with one (rather than multiple) providers, sentiments shared by another interviewee: "In the past you would go for screening and then you would go to another health unit ... for family planning …nowadays I come here, and I do screening and vFP in the same place and the nurse doesn't change.
I feel more comfortable, because they are intimate matters that the fewer people know the better."

(Client, Jose Macamo health facility, Maputo city) For these clients, being seen by the same provider in a single location during the same visit not only made the service more convenient, but was also more psychologically comfortable, allowing a greater feeling of confidentiality around issues she considers sensitive.

This theme emerged elsewhere: "Let's say I want to use the IUD planning method -I would have to undress in front of a person ...and then have to go to another room to undress again for another person and it is a bit embarrassing.
Now if it is to do both things with the same person for me it is more advantageous" (Client, Mavalane health facility, Maputo city)
The perceived embarrassment of seeing health providers for SRHR-related services was reduced through having those services integrated into a single consultation.

Providers also identified the improved privacy of a single visit as a key benefit of integration: "[Clients] really fear removing clothes in front of people, so that is why they are more comfortable with this [integrated] service model" (Nurse, Jose Macamo health facility in Maputo city) Key informant interviews with clinic staff show that they also consider integrated services to be more convenient for their clients.

One commented: "The patients here have two services in one office so they come and they can do the vFP and the screening consecutively because it is also a constraint that [otherwise] she is in the family planning queue and after that queue is over, she comes to do the screening" (Provider, Jose Macamo health facility, Maputo city)

text.text: In addition to convenience and privacy, some clients interviewed discussed how integration means learning about, and taking up services that they might not have been aware of otherwise: "The mixed services have a greater effect than separate ones because many people who come for [family] planning end up being informed about screening and end up doing this and it is very good" (Client, Chibuto health facility, Gaza province) Some issues and barriers to accessing integrated services emerged through in-depth interviews, however: "I think that they could take us who come for treatment out of the queue of people coming for screening and family planning for the first time, because we know where we are coming from and what we want while another group is coming for the first time and we are in the same queue, sometimes I feel pain because of sitting too much on those hospital benches."
(Client, Chicumbana health facility, Gaza province) Waiting times are an issue for this client, for whom the return visit for treatment involved having to wait alongside those being screened.

From the providers' perspectives, the integration of vFP and CCS&PT services resulted in some unexpected outcomes: "Because of the integration of services, I have noticed that most women have started to worry about their health, and some even bring their friends and even neighbors to the hospital for family planning and screening.

text.text: Overall, we found high levels of uptake of integrated services among women enrolled in CCS&PT in the four public health facilities (in Maputo City and Gaza province), with almost 9 in 10 women who were enrolled for cervical cancer screening with hrHPV test also receiving vFP counselling on the day of their visit.

text.text: Increased uptake of vFP when services are integrated has been observed elsewhere -including in Kenya, where HIV and vFP integration showed significant increases in FP method use (Chen et al., 2020).

text.text: Around one in five women in this study who received these integrated services took up a contraceptive method on the day of their visit.
These data suggest that offering vFP services to women who attend CCS&PT services in Mozambique is a feasible intervention, a finding supported by a recent systematic review (Bulstra et al., 2021).

text.text: This presents an opportunity to improve access for women with unmet needs; one in five of the women taking up a contraceptive method were new users.

Clients who had accessed integrated services expressed a high degree of satisfaction with the convenience, enhanced privacy, reduced wait time and travel costs and opportunity to learn about new services that this model presents.
Client satisfaction has been identified elsewhere to be an important driver of vFP service uptake (Paine et al., 2000) and a determinant of quality (Tessema et al., 2016).

text.text: We found evidence of some sensitivity around sexual and reproductive health and rights service provision and exposure to providers among some interviewees.
These understandable concerns were mitigated for many by an integrated model in which clients see a single provider for both vFP and CCS&PT.
text.formatted: These understandable concerns were mitigated for many by an integrated model in which clients see a single provider for both vFP and CCS&PT.

text.text: Further advantages, such as reduced time taken visiting health centers and reduced time waiting in queues within them were also important, particularly in the Mozambiquan context where transportation options to get to health centers for many clients may be limited, and the opportunity costs of multiple health center visits for those working in the informal economy, for example, may be considerable.
Providers who were involved in integrated service delivery expressed similar views to many clients concerning privacy and convenience.

In addition, providers also discussed the impact that integrated services (and particularly clients having a positive experience) could have on increasing demand for these health services through peer referrals.

The benefit of combining and making accessible vFP and CCS&PT for women in Mozambique has the potential to extend beyond a client, to her community and wider social network, including through wordof-mouth peer referrals.

text.text: Ensuring that services are truly integrated seems to be an important lesson from this research.
Calls for sexual and reproductive health services to be brought fully and intentionally into universal health care (Appleford et al., 2020) in the literature support this conclusion.
text.formatted: Calls for sexual and reproductive health services to be brought fully and intentionally into universal health care <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Appleford et al., 2020)</ref> in the literature support this conclusion.

text.text: The key advantages stem from clients being able to see a single provider, in a single session, for both services.
Other integration models involve multiple providers within the same clinic, and indeed one client discussed the inconvenience of having to queue for two separate sessions on the same visit.
Future service provision should consider ensuring a clientcentered, fully integrated model as the ideal approach.

Finally, while Mozambique's national policy framework highlights the importance of providing integrated SRHR services, different models of integration exist, and practical implementation of an integrated model requires physical and administrative infrastructure that is not always prioritized in busy, clinical environments.
Our study suggests that there may be efficiencies in full integrated services for both clients and providers, which might counter the upfront set-up effort.
This study has several limitations.
First, the quantitative component relied on routine program data, with a challenge of missing data for some self-reported socio-demographic variables.

Second, because this operational research was nested within a larger clinical trial, all participants in the study were recruited for CCS&PT; our definition of integration here therefore means the inclusion of vFP within a CCS&PT service provision model.

text.text: We cannot comment therefore on the uptake or feasibility of a model where CCS&PT services are provided within an existing system of vFP service provision.

text.text: Nevertheless, we did analyze clients' self-reported original reason for clinic attendance, and a substantial minority reported attending for vFP, rather than CCS&PT.

text.text: A final limitation regards the generalizability of the quantitative data, given the study population of those eligible for CCS&PT.

text.text: Further research, outside of a clinical trial context would be useful to establish the degree to which our findings may apply to other groups of women in Mozambique.
Integration of vFP into CCS&PT services resulted in increased overall vFP uptake, with a substantial minority of women taking up vFP for the first time through the integrated model.

text.text: Our results suggest integration of these services is appealing to both women and providers, as it offers greater convenience, privacy, and fewer clinic visits.

The implementation and potential scale-up of this model in Mozambique could represent a mutually beneficial opportunity to increase both access and uptake to voluntary family planning and cervical cancer screening and could result in increased efficiency in providing access to products and services that improve women's sexual and reproductive health in ways that align with existing policy and are responsive to women's needs.

text.text: Mozambique's Strategic Health Plan for 2014 to 2019, extending to at least 2024 (MISAU, 2022) established the promotion of universal health care, with a focus on Primary Health Care, while the most recent 2023-2030 National Family Planning strategy calls specifically for the expansion of integrated vFP services (Direcção Nacional de Saúde Pública, 2023).
This means providing integrated and continuous services that are accessible, locally relevant and acceptable, with appropriate technology, participation and community ownership.
The program includes the integration of cervical cancer screening into sexual and reproductive health (SRH) programs.

In 2009, the Mozambique Ministry of Health initiated the program for prevention of cervical and breast cancer, having already established basic cervical cancer screening services in 75 health facilities in country.
Despite policy level efforts to promote both CCS&PT and service integration more widely, anecdotal evidence suggests implementation of this policy is patchy.

text.text: This manuscript presents evidence from operational research conducted as part of the Partnership for Enhanced Engagement Research (PEER) project in Mozambique and MULHER Study, in which vFP services were integrated into CCS&PT services in four public health facilities as part of a larger clinical trial of CCS&PT diagnostics and treatments

text.text: Partnership for Enhanced Engagement Research (PEER) was a collaborative project between Eduardo Mondlane University Faculty of Medicine (UEM), The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center (MD Anderson), the United States Agency for International Development and National Academy of Science, Engineering and Medicine (USAID/NASEM) and Population Services International (PSI), to generate evidence to inform national and global efforts to scale-up effective and efficient cervical cancer screening and treatment programs.

The consortium aimed to evaluate the impact of integration of cervical cancer prevention into existing vFP programs in Mozambique, while testing the feasibility and acceptability of innovative point of care molecular diagnostic tests for detection of high-risk human papillomavirus (hrHPV), and to strengthen capacity to implement these CCS&PT interventions more efficiently and effectively at scale.
